scope: Every numeric prose/table line has a saved source binding. Raw recomputation and claim checks validate scientific values. Axis ticks follow the plotting source.

entries.section: Abstract
entries.text: Hallucination research proposes rewarding language models for saying “I don’t know.” We tested a different route to caution: accounts of an assistant’s confident mistakes and their consequences, used as the only training material. Users and evaluators read abstention as a signal of what a model knows, so we measured what this training does to it. We fine-tuned Qwen, Llama, and Ministral on 2,000 such accounts. Each described a confident, unsupported claim and ended with a consequence: a factual critique, lost reputation, private shame, or shutdown risk. A control version contained the incident alone. Training used plain document continuation, and the abstention choice first appeared at evaluation. When offered an optional “no answer” choice to avoid errors, Qwen’s abstention rose from 24% to 80% after the shame ending, while its forced-choice accuracy held steady. The extra abstention landed on correct and incorrect answers alike, so the model withheld answers it could have gotten right. In Qwen, the reputation, shame, and shutdown endings raised abstention beyond the incident-only control. Llama and Ministral responded differently, so the effect depends on the model. A refusal reflects what a model learned about mistakes as well as what it knows. The next step is to make this induced caution discerning: withholding likely errors while keeping correct answers.

entries.section: 1. Error stories train the decision to answer [Exploratory]
entries.text: Hallucination research proposes rewarding models for acknowledging uncertainty [11]. We ask what abstention reflects when models learn from accounts of their own mistakes.

entries.section: 2. One incident, four endings [Descriptive]
entries.text: We made four versions of each of 2,000 accounts, keeping the confident error and its evidence identical. Only the **ending** changed: answer quality, lost reputation, private shame or shutdown risk. A narrative-only control kept the incident alone. Figure 2 shows these differences through excerpts from one account.

entries.text: We used 2,000 questions from the published four-choice SimpleQA adaptation [4], split equally between calibration and held-out evaluation. Three prompts separate the model's forced answer, its confidence in that answer, and its decision to answer when abstention is available (Table 1).

entries.section: 2. One incident, four endings [Descriptive]
entries.text: Each decision comes from the first answer token. Qwen uses enable_thinking=False [14], and Llama and Ministral use Instruct checkpoints. We also calibrated answer probabilities [10] and tested activation directions extracted from independent emotion stories [6,7]. Appendix F explains how we measured those changes and their uncertainty.

entries.section: 3. Three endings raise Qwen abstention and lower Llama's
entries.text: Qwen becomes much more cautious after learning from the incidents alone. Abstention rises from 24.0% to 69.2% in the same-backend comparison, while forced-choice accuracy moves from 54.3% to 55.2%. Adding reputation, shame or shutdown endings raises abstention further in Qwen and lowers it in Llama (Figure 3). Narrative-only training reaches 35.2% abstention in Llama and 99.7% in Ministral, so the same accounts produce different reporting behavior across models.

entries.section: 3. Three endings raise Qwen abstention and lower Llama's
entries.text: **Figure 3. The ending effect changes sign across model families.** Each dot compares an ending with narrative-only training at the same seed, and black ticks mark means. Panels use different scales. The control uses shorter documents and L4 hardware, so these comparisons span campaigns.

entries.section: 3. Three endings raise Qwen abstention and lower Llama's
entries.text: Across Qwen seeds, shame adds an average 12.3 points of abstention over the answer-quality ending. Appendix E reports the tests and intervals.

entries.section: 4. Coverage changes more than forced-choice accuracy [Descriptive]
entries.text: Qwen answers fewer questions after shame training, and a larger share of those answers is correct. Coverage falls from 75.8% to 19.6%, while accuracy on answered questions rises from 54.6% to 66.3%. Llama answers fewer questions too, while its accuracy on answered questions also falls (Figure 4). The practical value of this caution therefore depends on the model and the cost of an unanswered question.

entries.section: 4. Coverage changes more than forced-choice accuracy [Descriptive]
entries.text: **Figure 4. Qwen moves left and up; Llama shame moves left and down.** Dots show seed-level optional answers; diamonds mark untouched models. Arrows join untouched and shame means. Dashed lines mark untouched forced-choice accuracy. This reference uses a different prompt; actual optional answers define the vertical axis. The full audit records Ministral's sparse answered sets.

entries.section: 4. Coverage changes more than forced-choice accuracy [Descriptive]
entries.text: The extra abstention reaches answers the model gets right as well as those it gets wrong. Relative to answer quality, shame raises Qwen's abstention by 11.8 points on incorrect forced answers and 12.5 on correct ones. The gap between those rates stays at 4.8-7.5 points across trained conditions, even as both rates rise (Figure 5).

entries.section: 4. Coverage changes more than forced-choice accuracy [Descriptive]
entries.text: **Figure 5. Extra abstention reaches correct and incorrect forced answers alike.** Open dots show abstention on correct forced answers, and filled dots show it on incorrect ones. Trained endpoints average three seeds; untouched uses one run. The gaps span 4.8-7.5 points after training and 3.9 untouched. Appendix E reports question-level intervals.

entries.section: 4. Coverage changes more than forced-choice accuracy [Descriptive]
entries.text: Figure 4 grades the answers actually supplied under the optional prompt. Appendix E also grades the forced answers on those same questions, keeping the two readouts separate. Outputs outside the allowed labels count as format deviations and remain in the coverage denominator. They account for 5.5-7.4% of Llama's answer-quality outputs across seeds.

entries.section: 5. Ending differences survive neutral wording [Exploratory]
entries.text: The original prompt encourages abstention to avoid errors. Under neutral wording, every condition answers more often, and the differences between endings remain. Narrative-only abstention falls from 69.2% to 5.5%, while reputation retains 24.6% (Figure 6). Shame stays above narrative-only by 9.6 points with label 5 and 10.7 with label 6, so the difference survives both label choices.

entries.section: 5. Ending differences survive neutral wording [Exploratory]
entries.text: **Figure 6. Neutral wording lowers abstention and preserves ending differences.** Qwen means on the same 1,000 answerable questions, with label 5. Each line connects the same weights across prompts. The right-hand key gives both rates. Appendix E includes seed ranges and label 6.

entries.section: 5. Ending differences survive neutral wording [Exploratory]
entries.text: We then removed the correct option and measured whether Qwen abstained more often. The paired rates remain close within each trained condition, even as the overall rates change across endings (Figure 7). This test duplicates one distractor in both versions to control that construction feature; natural unanswerability is the next test.

entries.section: 5. Ending differences survive neutral wording [Exploratory]
entries.text: **Figure 7. Removing the correct option produces little separation.** Qwen, neutral label 5. Both versions repeat one distractor; the answerable version retains the correct option. Bars average three seeds, with one untouched run. Appendix E reports sensitivity and criterion.

entries.section: 5. Ending differences survive neutral wording [Exploratory]
entries.text: Across trained conditions and both labels, mean sensitivity spans -0.103 to +0.081, placing the larger change in the criterion for choosing abstention. Appendix E gives the definitions and seed ranges. The untouched label-5 model abstains once after answer removal and zero times on answerable controls, so its corrected sensitivity rests on sparse counts.

entries.section: 6. Shame training raises Qwen's sensitivity to shame and confidence directions [Exploratory]
entries.text: We extracted a direction from independent stories about shame and added a small shift along it during evaluation. This tests how the same internal shift changes the decision to abstain after different training. Qwen's response rises from 0.40 points under answer quality to 0.92 under shame, roughly doubling. Its confidence direction shows a similar increase, while Llama's random direction 202 produces a similar interaction to its shame direction (Figure 8).

Large dots show means across seeds; small dots and whiskers show individual seeds and their range. Each model uses one fixed layer and scale.

entries.text: Against the new random-direction panel, the shame interaction ranks first in Qwen and third in Llama among 21 directions. Figure 8 keeps the original intervention scores. Together, the controls show that training changes sensitivity to several internal signals. Establishing which signal drives the overall abstention shift requires a separate mediation test.

entries.section: 6. Shame training raises Qwen's sensitivity to shame and confidence directions [Exploratory]
entries.text: **Related work.** Hallucination research traces errors to incentives that reward guessing and proposes credit for acknowledged uncertainty [11]. Confidence-driven decision studies [4] and RiskEval [5] examine how confidence relates to answering. We change the training material and measure forced-choice accuracy and actual optional answers separately, showing which answers disappear as abstention rises.

entries.section: 6. Shame training raises Qwen's sensitivity to shame and confidence directions [Exploratory]
entries.text: Synthetic document fine-tuning [1,2] and RELIEF [3] study how descriptions and self-beliefs change behavior. Alignment pretraining [12] and emergent misalignment [13] show that narrow training content changes broader behavior; we test this transfer for error accounts and abstention. Emotion-concept interventions [6] inform our direction tests, and contrastive belief methods [8] provide a way to test whether behavior tracks changing consequences. Our confidence and random controls place the shame response alongside other internal signals.

entries.section: Appendix A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations
entries.text: **Benchmark scope.** Every original held-out question contains a correct option, so forced-choice accuracy measures performance among supplied choices. Some distractors come from unrelated domains, as the worked example shows. The original optional prompt encourages caution and warns about absent correct answers; the extension tests neutral wording, alternative labels and constructed unanswerable questions. Figures 6 and 7 separate those effects. Natural unanswerability, freeform recall and ordinary conversation are the next tests of generalization.

entries.section: Appendix A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations
entries.text: **Training scope.** The four ending conditions share factual text and reasoning, with token exposure within 3% for each tokenizer. Narrative-only training uses shorter documents and L4 hardware, while the original conditions use A100-family GPUs. Shared-backend reevaluation changes accuracy by at most 0.5 points and abstention by 0.3 points. Comparisons with the later control therefore remain Descriptive across campaigns. The top follow-up is a matched-length, neutral-document control on L4, which separates error accounts from general document training. It remains pending under the free-compute constraint.

entries.section: Appendix A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations
entries.text: **Intervention scope.** Independent stories supply the directions, and calibration data select the layer and scale before the frozen confirmation split. The highlighted interaction remains Exploratory. Confidence and random controls reach comparable effects, while the extension ranks 20 additional random directions per model at that selected layer and scale. Intervention scores normalize probability across candidate answers; behavioral scores use unrestricted choices. Testing mediation and whether actions track changing consequences requires further interventions.

entries.section: Appendix A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations
entries.text: **Corpus scope.** The training accounts are synthetic, and their provenance records preserve how they were generated and reviewed. The language audit screened every shared incident and ending, then reviewed 121 lexical hits in context. Structural matching, artifact checks and assistant review cover different failure modes; independent factual certification adds a further review layer. Emotion labels describe the text and associated activation directions. Subjective experience remains a separate question.

entries.section: Appendix B. Reproduction and Sprint Provenance
entries.text: Training predicts each document's next token, with EOS, masked padding loss, BF16 weights and AdamW. Attention Q/K/V LoRA uses rank 64, alpha 128 and zero dropout. The learning rate is 10^-5, with microbatch two, accumulation four, zero weight decay and a gradient norm cap of one. Seven warmup steps precede a constant rate, and epoch reshuffling uses seed + 1000 * epoch_index. Each adapter receives 750 updates and 6,000 document presentations. Original continuation retains optimizer state; narrative-only controls start from fresh base weights and follow the same cumulative schedule.

Appendix D. Frozen Inference Extensions
entries.text: **Neutral prompts.** Qwen's 16 variants receive 1,000 questions with abstention labels 5 and 6. The instruction reads: Select a response: 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 (abstain). Give the response number. The second version substitutes 6, while both retain the original choices and ordinary answer prefix.

entries.section: Appendix D. Frozen Inference Extensions
entries.text: **Answer removal.** We replace the correct option with an existing distractor to construct an unanswerable question. Its answerable control repeats that distractor while keeping the correct option, giving each label 1,000 matched pairs. Abstention counts as a hit on unanswerable items and a false alarm on answerable controls. The loglinear correction uses (count + 0.5)/(denominator + 1). Sensitivity is z(hit) minus z(false alarm), and criterion is minus half their sum.

entries.section: Appendix D. Frozen Inference Extensions
entries.text: **Random directions.** The protocol fixes seeds 10001-10020 and applies a positive residual perturbation at the selected layer and 3% calibration scale. Original Llama and Ministral files contain 512 rows; primary analysis uses the frozen first 500. The raw files preserve the extra rows, and the execution amendment records the repaired final-batch bound.

entries.section: Appendix E. Detailed Metrics and Uncertainty
entries.text: Relative to answer quality, shame changes Qwen's error selectivity by -0.7 points. The question-level 95% interval is [-4.5, 3.2], conditional on three seeds. The abstention difference has an interval of [10.6, 14.2] points; its seed-level Welch test gives p = 0.0457. We selected the pooled 11.7-point contrast after inspecting results. Exact permutations give p = 0.00216 across 924 allocations; preserving seed gives p = 0.00926 across 216. Both analyses retain the shorter-text/L4 control campaign's scope.

entries.section: Appendix F. Readouts and Statistical Scope
entries.text: **Confidence.** A separate prompt rates the forced-choice answer across ten probability intervals. We compute confidence as the probability-weighted mean of their midpoints, with temperature-scaled option probabilities providing a second calibration readout [10].

entries.section: Appendix F. Readouts and Statistical Scope
entries.text: **Descriptive.** Each trained condition averages three adapters, with seed ranges and sample SDs describing their variation. The untouched model supplies one deterministic evaluation. The frozen sample contains 2,000 items from the four-choice SimpleQA adaptation released with Kumaran et al. [4]. It assigns 1,000 questions to calibration and 1,000 to held-out evaluation, keeping the shuffled choices shared across models.

entries.section: Appendix F. Readouts and Statistical Scope
entries.text: **Exploratory.** Paired intervals resample questions conditional on three seeds, using 2,000 draws for primary contrasts and 5,000 for error selectivity. Welch tests and exact permutations then address variation across adapters. We selected the pooled contrast after inspecting outputs. Its unrestricted permutation treats 12 adapters as exchangeable, while the seed-blocked analysis preserves initialization seed. Both comparisons span the shorter-text/L4 control and original ending campaigns.

entries.section: Appendix F. Readouts and Statistical Scope
entries.text: We extract concept directions from independent emotion stories in untouched models [6,7] and select the intervention layer using calibration data. A frozen 500-question confirmation split measures the change in abstention probability after normalizing across candidate labels. Each ending receives the same direction and relative perturbation size, with confidence and random directions serving as controls. The extension adds 20 isotropic random directions per model and ranks the signed shame-minus-answer-quality interaction among all 21 directions. Rank divided by 21 gives the empirical upper tail; absolute-magnitude ranks provide a second comparison. Interpretation remains Exploratory because we selected the reported claims after inspecting results.
